title: Changes in Polyamine Metabolism in Response to Abiotic Stress

sections.abstract: Polyamine metabolism and function in plant cells have many elements in common with the processes studied in microbial and animal systems. For example, plant and bacterial cells share the existence of alternate pathways for putrescine synthesis, mediated by arginine (ADC) and ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), respectively. Many of the roles ascribed to plant polyamines in plants are also essentially those proposed for other systems, such as control of the cell cycle, cell division and morphogenesis. Polyamines in plant systems, however, have several unique features; the sharing of a common precursor for polyamine and ethylene biosynthesis, the widespread occurrence of hydroxycinnamic acid conjugates, and the existence of over 1000 poly amine-derived alkaloids are some of the metabolic features found only in plant species (see Chapters 4 and 5). Polyamines have been involved in functions which only occur in plant systems, such as phytochrome and plant hormone-mediated processes, and control of plant senescence; these are reviewed in Chapters 13 and 14, respectively. The oldest known and perhaps the most dramatic changes in polyamine metabolism which characterize plant cells are those obtained when plants are challenged with abiotic stresses. Although the functional significance of these responses is not fully understood, it is clear that major shifts in nitrogen and polyamine metabolism can occur when plant cells are starved for nutrients, or exposed to low pH, osmotic shock or environmental pollutants. In this chapter, we will review the physiology and biochemistry of these and other changes. Several recent reviews have covered some of these aspects. 1-3 Polyamine metabolism can also be affected when plants are exposed to biotic stress, involving mainly exposure to plant pathogenic fungi and viruses. Because these alterations involve mostly polyamine-derived secondary metabolites, they will not be covered in this review (see Chapter 4). Discussions of polyamines and stress responses have also been related to their metabolic/functional antagonism with ethylene and their possible role as antisenescence compounds; these topics are covered in Chapters 5 and 15, respectively.
